quote: "No man is more unhappy than he who never faces adversity. For he is not permitted to prove himself." — Seneca, On Providence
context:
Seneca wrote On Providence to answer a hard objection from his friend Lucilius: if the world is governed by a rational order, why do good people suffer? His reply refuses the easy comfort. He argues that hardship is not evidence of abandonment but the only arena in which character becomes visible. A person spared every difficulty, in his account, is like an untested soldier or an athlete with no opponent: not fortunate, but deprived. Strength that is never called on is only a rumor of strength. The essay treats trial as the condition under which a life proves what it is made of, rather than a flaw in how the world is run.


This week Alexander Zverev won his first US Open title, beating Ben Shelton in a four-set final, his second major of the year and the close of a redemption arc six years in the making.
 The wins matter, but Seneca points somewhere quieter: the value was already accruing in the years of losing finals. The difficulty did not delay the man he became. It made him.
question: What has your hardest stretch shown you about yourself that an easier one never could have?
